text: This lesson pulls together Chapter 4's emissions, farming, and vault mechanics with this chapter's supply math into one question: where does the yield actually come from? A few warning signs the answer is nowhere sustainable follow.

Rewards paid entirely in the protocol's own inflationary token with no path to real revenue. Advertised APY dramatically exceeding any plausible real usage revenue. No token sink removing supply to offset new emissions. And new deposits required to keep paying existing depositors — structurally the same shape as a Ponzi scheme, intentional or not.

Compare two protocols. Protocol A advertises 150% APY, sourced entirely from newly minted governance tokens — real revenue this year is only $50,000, but tokens emitted are worth $15,000,000. That yield is backed almost entirely by new issuance, not revenue.

Protocol B advertises a smaller 8%, sourced entirely from trading fees paid in USDC and ETH, no new minting at all. Real revenue this year is $2,400,000, and that's exactly what gets paid out to stakers. Every dollar paid already exists as revenue, independent of the token's price.

Protocol A's 150% only holds up as long as the token's price survives $15,000,000 a year in new supply — exactly the sell-pressure spiral from Lesson 16 that tends to collapse the number. Protocol B's 8% is smaller but durable.

A sustainable design pays real yield from fees wherever possible, caps and tapers emissions with an end date, builds in token sinks like burns and lockups, and matches lock duration to reward duration. Next: modeling how token supply and demand actually interact over time.
